medical.title: New tool measures thyroid cancer patients' anxiety
medical.summary: A new tool created by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University investigators is the first to measure anxiety in patients with thyroid cancer. Described in the journal Thyroid, the Thyroid Cancer Modified Anxiety Scale (TC-MAX) could help doctors clarify patients' expectations, better match treatment to their needs and improve patient outcomes.

medical.title: Small bowel microbiome offers clues to women's health
medical.summary: A new study by investigators at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University has identified differences in the makeup and organization of the small bowel microbiome between women and men. The findings, published in iScience, could offer new insights into why some conditions are more prevalent in women.

medical.title: Why do I crash at 3pm? The science behind the 'afternoon slump'
medical.summary: You've just finished eating lunch and you're back at your desk, ready to dive into the rest of the day's work. Yet by 3 p.m., you find your eyes starting to droop. Before long, the only thing you can think about is how much you'd like to take a nap.

medical.title: AI helps clarify complex array and interaction of risk factors contributing to alcohol use disorder
medical.summary: Explainable AI (xAI) models are illuminating the multiple risk factors that underlie the development of alcohol use disorder (AUD), according to a new study. Although some factors involved in AUD—including demographic, socioeconomic and genetic variables—are known, researchers typically study them in isolation, and their roles in individuals' risk are often small. The variability of AUD presentations, meanwhile, reflects unique personal combinations of genetic, environmental, neurobiological and psychosocial factors. Understanding their relative influence and how these variables interact could better predict the risk of dangerous drinking and inform tailored prevention and treatment approaches.

medical.title: Targeted school intervention outperforms media lessons for teens at risk of gaming disorder
medical.summary: School-based prevention programs are designed to help protect adolescents from gaming disorder and problematic online habits. But how effective are these interventions in promoting responsible use of video games and the internet?

medical.title: How the mouse brain learns from a single experience
medical.summary: Sometimes, even a single experience can be highly impactful, prompting humans and other animals to change their behavior or influencing their future choices. The formation of influential memories from a single, brief experience is also known as one-shot learning.

medical.title: Researchers find sex-specific benefits of experimental stroke therapy
medical.summary: Researchers at the FAMU-FSU College of Engineering and National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, or MagLab, have shown that a potential stroke treatment derived from stem cells may be more effective for women.

medical.title: Why scientists are looking to provoke disagreement among AI brain models
medical.summary: When people wanted to create better artificial intelligence, they looked to the brain for inspiration. Now the tables are turning, and researchers are using AI models to better understand the brain. But how do we judge which AI models might accurately describe the computations the brain is performing?

medical.title: Reducing unnecessary fluid testing could lower cancer care costs
medical.summary: Doctors might be able to safely reduce health care costs by skipping unnecessary laboratory tests for patients with advanced gynecologic cancers, according to a Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University study. The paper, published in JAMA Network Open, examined testing on fluid drained from the abdomen or around the lungs.

medical.title: Why beauty feels shared: Brain scans map art's content and pleasure pathways
medical.summary: Stand in front of "Turner's Sun Rising Over Water" (1825–30), and something odd tends to happen. The painting holds you, even though observers might struggle to say why. Maybe it is the color, the balance, the composition or the strange stillness the artwork seems to carry.

medical.title: How deep sleep shapes mental resilience to stressful situations
medical.summary: Most adult sleep is non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep, which is restorative and promotes resilience to stressful conditions. However, the brain mechanisms underlying non-REM sleep's relationship to stress resilience remain unclear. New in JNeurosci, Christopher Ehlen of Morehouse School of Medicine and colleagues explored how cortical brain activity in mice during non-REM sleep influences behavioral responses to stressful social situations.

medical.title: Markers of chronic disease discovered in young, healthy drinkers
medical.summary: Alcohol use appears to trigger specific biological changes in the human body that are linked to the development of chronic disease. These biological changes are already apparent in young adults with a short history of alcohol consumption. A new study published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research found specific biomarkers of chronic disease across multiple biological systems related to both immediate and long-term alcohol use patterns.

medical.title: Targeting mosquitoes reduces flesh-eating ulcer risk in Melbourne trial
medical.summary: Mosquito control in an urban setting can reduce a person's risk of contracting Buruli ulcer by over 80%, finds a new Melbourne-led study.

medical.title: How the heart, lungs and brain work together to shape experience
medical.summary: People speak of "butterflies in the stomach," a "racing heart," being "choked up" or needing to "catch breath." Language routinely treats emotion and thought as though they inhabit the body. But why are events of the mind felt in the heart or stomach?

medical.title: Caregivers for people with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder report increased stress and relational strengths
medical.summary: Caregivers of people with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) identified stress levels and emotional health as the factors most negatively affected by their caregiving role. Many experienced limited social support and financial and employment challenges because of their caregiver role. These findings, just published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research, highlight the need for policies and programs that support families and caregivers of children and adults with developmental disabilities in general, and FASD in particular.

science.title: 'The Jungle Book' offers an unconventional tool for undergraduate economics education
science.summary: Research in the International Journal of Pluralism and Economics Education argues that "The Jungle Book" can serve as an unconventional teaching tool for undergraduate economics, using the original stories by Rudyard Kipling as well as Disney film adaptations to introduce concepts ranging from scarcity and sustainability to happiness and development.

science.title: Weak hydrogen bonds dethrone copper as the most stable metal binder, opening a new path for metal selection
science.summary: Copper has been knocked off the top of a stability ranking it had dominated for decades. Without altering the atoms directly bonded to the metal, a KAIST research team reversed the longstanding trend in which copper generally forms the most stable complexes by tuning only the weak hydrogen bonds in its surrounding environment. The findings, which appear in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, could open new avenues for selective metal separation and recognition, as well as catalyst design.

science.title: Inexpensive blue pigment enables efficient one-step conversion of carbon dioxide to methane
science.summary: A common blue pigment could help turn carbon dioxide (CO₂) from an industrial waste product into a useful fuel. A joint research team led by Tohoku University's Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), in collaboration with Hokkaido University and startup AZUL Energy, has developed a catalyst that converts CO₂ directly into methane (CH₄) with high efficiency using copper phthalocyanine, an inexpensive and readily available blue pigment.

science.title: Ships, ice cores and krill surveys underpin Australia's 10-year Antarctic monitoring strategy
science.summary: The important role ships play in gathering scientific data in Antarctica and the Southern Ocean has been outlined at a leading Antarctic science conference in Hobart. The biennial Australian Antarctic Research Conference was held at the University of Tasmania and attracted 400 researchers from around the globe.

science.title: Why 'you're smart' can backfire: Young children may cheat more after ability praise
science.summary: Parents and teachers might think telling kids "they're smart" is a helpful way to build self-confidence and support positive development.

science.title: Stripped-down LSD reveals structural features linked to hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects
science.summary: University of California, Davis, researchers have stripped down LSD to the base features responsible for its hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects.

science.title: New nitride semiconductor expands material options for more powerful electronics
science.summary: Polar wurtzite nitride semiconductors, such as aluminum nitride (AlN) and gallium nitride (GaN), are central to modern high-power and high-frequency electronic devices because of their wide band gaps, high breakdown electric fields, and strong spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization.

science.title: 'Heel-strike' may have allowed early humans to walk farther—at the cost of high-impact forces
science.summary: The average person takes thousands of steps each day, instinctively walking heel-to-toe. Although they hardly register them, those consistent heel-first strides are more distinctive to humans than previously thought and allowed early hominins to walk farther and more efficiently, but at the cost of higher impact forces on bones and joints, according to a new study led by a researcher at Penn State.

science.title: Slender crystal's blue-to-yellow glow could make invisible forces visible
science.summary: Applying pressure to luminescent organic crystals usually brings molecules closer together and weakens their fluorescence. Materials that instead brighten and undergo a large color change are rare, and clear design principles for achieving both responses in simple, rigid aromatic hydrocarbons have been lacking.

science.title: What can a pair of underpants tell you about your vegetable garden?
science.summary: This summer, 115 participants in Leiden and The Hague worked with scientists from Leiden University to investigate the soil life in their community garden plots. With mangetout peas, a taste test, a buried pair of underpants and a harvest festival, they helped scientists better understand the connection between soil, plants and people.

science.title: Reversible electric control unlocks persistent chiral phonon states
science.summary: Atoms in a material are rarely still. They jiggle back and forth in collective lattice vibrations known as phonons. Their motion can also carry a rotational element: In 2023, scientists at PSI experimentally proved the existence of chiral phonons, which exhibit handedness depending on which way they rotate.

science.title: Entangled particles revive a 35-year-old test of the Standard Model
science.summary: Physicists at the BESIII Collaboration have breathed new life into a decades-old test of one of the Standard Model's most important ideas, using a technique that had gone almost untouched by experimenters for 35 years.

science.title: Organic farming outperforms wildflower strips on profits while both improve farm biodiversity
science.summary: What makes more sense when farming wheat—strips of wildflowers along fields or organic farming? Both options provide financial support via the European Union as environmentally friendly and sustainable farming practices. An international research team, including researchers from the University of Göttingen, has compared the ecological and economic benefits of these two farming methods in fields planted with winter wheat.

science.title: Self-processing brain systems show both conservation and reorganization across primates
science.summary: New in JNeurosci, Ning Liu, from the Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, explored whether brain structures for self-processing are conserved across primates, including humans, chimpanzees and macaques.

science.title: Excavations at Prado Vargas now span 140 square meters of a Neanderthal layer
science.summary: The 2026 field season at Prado Vargas Cave, located in the village of Cornejo in the northern province of Burgos, Spain, within the Ojo Guareña karst complex, has expanded the excavation of Neanderthal sublevel 4D by 32 square meters (344 square feet), bringing the total excavated area to 140 square meters (1,507 square feet). More than 1,500 animal remains and stone tools were recovered, strengthening the interpretation of this roughly 46,000-year-old layer as a large Neanderthal camp.

science.title: Could bats self-medicate? More than 50 wild bats offer clues
science.summary: When humans get sick, we change our routines and try various solutions to feel better and get well, like staying in bed to rest, going to the doctor, getting medication from the pharmacy, using home remedies and more.

science.title: Dark plasma regions reveal overlooked source of reactive atomic oxygen
science.summary: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have found a way to make plasma more effective for its wide-ranging uses, from antimicrobial applications to surface conditioning in the semiconductor industry. They mapped the production of atomic oxygen, a key ingredient of oxygen plasma, while a high voltage was applied across oxygen gas.

science.title: Galileo, Copernicus, Cleansky, IRIS² must work together to secure Europe's place in the space race
science.summary: "Seeing the Earth from above is a powerful reminder of our interdependence," said Thomas Pesquet. The words of France's 10th astronaut to head into space are a reminder of how we are "in this together," something the world's aerospace industry players should take heed of as they gather in Paris for the first International Space Summit from Sept. 9–10.

environment.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
environment.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. environment.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
environment.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: Research in the International Journal of Pluralism and Economics Education argues that "The Jungle Book" can serve as an unconventional teaching tool for undergraduate economics, using the original stories by Rudyard Kipling as well as Disney film adaptations to introduce concepts ranging from scarcity and sustainability to happiness and development.

mix_items.title: Weak hydrogen bonds dethrone copper as the most stable metal binder, opening a new path for metal selection
mix_items.summary: Copper has been knocked off the top of a stability ranking it had dominated for decades. Without altering the atoms directly bonded to the metal, a KAIST research team reversed the longstanding trend in which copper generally forms the most stable complexes by tuning only the weak hydrogen bonds in its surrounding environment. The findings, which appear in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, could open new avenues for selective metal separation and recognition, as well as catalyst design.

mix_items.title: New tool measures thyroid cancer patients' anxiety
mix_items.summary: A new tool created by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University investigators is the first to measure anxiety in patients with thyroid cancer. Described in the journal Thyroid, the Thyroid Cancer Modified Anxiety Scale (TC-MAX) could help doctors clarify patients' expectations, better match treatment to their needs and improve patient outcomes.

mix_items.title: Inexpensive blue pigment enables efficient one-step conversion of carbon dioxide to methane
mix_items.summary: A common blue pigment could help turn carbon dioxide (CO₂) from an industrial waste product into a useful fuel. A joint research team led by Tohoku University's Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), in collaboration with Hokkaido University and startup AZUL Energy, has developed a catalyst that converts CO₂ directly into methane (CH₄) with high efficiency using copper phthalocyanine, an inexpensive and readily available blue pigment.

mix_items.title: Small bowel microbiome offers clues to women's health
mix_items.summary: A new study by investigators at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University has identified differences in the makeup and organization of the small bowel microbiome between women and men. The findings, published in iScience, could offer new insights into why some conditions are more prevalent in women.

mix_items.title: Ships, ice cores and krill surveys underpin Australia's 10-year Antarctic monitoring strategy
mix_items.summary: The important role ships play in gathering scientific data in Antarctica and the Southern Ocean has been outlined at a leading Antarctic science conference in Hobart. The biennial Australian Antarctic Research Conference was held at the University of Tasmania and attracted 400 researchers from around the globe.

mix_items.title: Why 'you're smart' can backfire: Young children may cheat more after ability praise
mix_items.summary: Parents and teachers might think telling kids "they're smart" is a helpful way to build self-confidence and support positive development.

mix_items.title: Stripped-down LSD reveals structural features linked to hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects
mix_items.summary: University of California, Davis, researchers have stripped down LSD to the base features responsible for its hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects.

mix_items.title: New nitride semiconductor expands material options for more powerful electronics
mix_items.summary: Polar wurtzite nitride semiconductors, such as aluminum nitride (AlN) and gallium nitride (GaN), are central to modern high-power and high-frequency electronic devices because of their wide band gaps, high breakdown electric fields, and strong spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization.

mix_items.title: 'Heel-strike' may have allowed early humans to walk farther—at the cost of high-impact forces
mix_items.summary: The average person takes thousands of steps each day, instinctively walking heel-to-toe. Although they hardly register them, those consistent heel-first strides are more distinctive to humans than previously thought and allowed early hominins to walk farther and more efficiently, but at the cost of higher impact forces on bones and joints, according to a new study led by a researcher at Penn State.

mix_items.title: Why do I crash at 3pm? The science behind the 'afternoon slump'
mix_items.summary: You've just finished eating lunch and you're back at your desk, ready to dive into the rest of the day's work. Yet by 3 p.m., you find your eyes starting to droop. Before long, the only thing you can think about is how much you'd like to take a nap.

mix_items.title: Slender crystal's blue-to-yellow glow could make invisible forces visible
mix_items.summary: Applying pressure to luminescent organic crystals usually brings molecules closer together and weakens their fluorescence. Materials that instead brighten and undergo a large color change are rare, and clear design principles for achieving both responses in simple, rigid aromatic hydrocarbons have been lacking.

mix_items.title: What can a pair of underpants tell you about your vegetable garden?
mix_items.summary: This summer, 115 participants in Leiden and The Hague worked with scientists from Leiden University to investigate the soil life in their community garden plots. With mangetout peas, a taste test, a buried pair of underpants and a harvest festival, they helped scientists better understand the connection between soil, plants and people.

mix_items.title: AI helps clarify complex array and interaction of risk factors contributing to alcohol use disorder
mix_items.summary: Explainable AI (xAI) models are illuminating the multiple risk factors that underlie the development of alcohol use disorder (AUD), according to a new study. Although some factors involved in AUD—including demographic, socioeconomic and genetic variables—are known, researchers typically study them in isolation, and their roles in individuals' risk are often small. The variability of AUD presentations, meanwhile, reflects unique personal combinations of genetic, environmental, neurobiological and psychosocial factors. Understanding their relative influence and how these variables interact could better predict the risk of dangerous drinking and inform tailored prevention and treatment approaches.

mix_items.title: Reversible electric control unlocks persistent chiral phonon states
mix_items.summary: Atoms in a material are rarely still. They jiggle back and forth in collective lattice vibrations known as phonons. Their motion can also carry a rotational element: In 2023, scientists at PSI experimentally proved the existence of chiral phonons, which exhibit handedness depending on which way they rotate.

mix_items.title: Targeted school intervention outperforms media lessons for teens at risk of gaming disorder
mix_items.summary: School-based prevention programs are designed to help protect adolescents from gaming disorder and problematic online habits. But how effective are these interventions in promoting responsible use of video games and the internet?

mix_items.title: How the mouse brain learns from a single experience
mix_items.summary: Sometimes, even a single experience can be highly impactful, prompting humans and other animals to change their behavior or influencing their future choices. The formation of influential memories from a single, brief experience is also known as one-shot learning.

mix_items.title: Entangled particles revive a 35-year-old test of the Standard Model
mix_items.summary: Physicists at the BESIII Collaboration have breathed new life into a decades-old test of one of the Standard Model's most important ideas, using a technique that had gone almost untouched by experimenters for 35 years.

mix_items.title: Researchers find sex-specific benefits of experimental stroke therapy
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the FAMU-FSU College of Engineering and National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, or MagLab, have shown that a potential stroke treatment derived from stem cells may be more effective for women.

mix_items.title: Organic farming outperforms wildflower strips on profits while both improve farm biodiversity
mix_items.summary: What makes more sense when farming wheat—strips of wildflowers along fields or organic farming? Both options provide financial support via the European Union as environmentally friendly and sustainable farming practices. An international research team, including researchers from the University of Göttingen, has compared the ecological and economic benefits of these two farming methods in fields planted with winter wheat.

mix_items.title: Why scientists are looking to provoke disagreement among AI brain models
mix_items.summary: When people wanted to create better artificial intelligence, they looked to the brain for inspiration. Now the tables are turning, and researchers are using AI models to better understand the brain. But how do we judge which AI models might accurately describe the computations the brain is performing?

mix_items.title: Reducing unnecessary fluid testing could lower cancer care costs
mix_items.summary: Doctors might be able to safely reduce health care costs by skipping unnecessary laboratory tests for patients with advanced gynecologic cancers, according to a Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University study. The paper, published in JAMA Network Open, examined testing on fluid drained from the abdomen or around the lungs.

mix_items.title: Self-processing brain systems show both conservation and reorganization across primates
mix_items.summary: New in JNeurosci, Ning Liu, from the Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, explored whether brain structures for self-processing are conserved across primates, including humans, chimpanzees and macaques.

mix_items.title: Why beauty feels shared: Brain scans map art's content and pleasure pathways
mix_items.summary: Stand in front of "Turner's Sun Rising Over Water" (1825–30), and something odd tends to happen. The painting holds you, even though observers might struggle to say why. Maybe it is the color, the balance, the composition or the strange stillness the artwork seems to carry.

mix_items.title: Excavations at Prado Vargas now span 140 square meters of a Neanderthal layer
mix_items.summary: The 2026 field season at Prado Vargas Cave, located in the village of Cornejo in the northern province of Burgos, Spain, within the Ojo Guareña karst complex, has expanded the excavation of Neanderthal sublevel 4D by 32 square meters (344 square feet), bringing the total excavated area to 140 square meters (1,507 square feet). More than 1,500 animal remains and stone tools were recovered, strengthening the interpretation of this roughly 46,000-year-old layer as a large Neanderthal camp.

mix_items.title: How deep sleep shapes mental resilience to stressful situations
mix_items.summary: Most adult sleep is non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep, which is restorative and promotes resilience to stressful conditions. However, the brain mechanisms underlying non-REM sleep's relationship to stress resilience remain unclear. New in JNeurosci, Christopher Ehlen of Morehouse School of Medicine and colleagues explored how cortical brain activity in mice during non-REM sleep influences behavioral responses to stressful social situations.

mix_items.title: Markers of chronic disease discovered in young, healthy drinkers
mix_items.summary: Alcohol use appears to trigger specific biological changes in the human body that are linked to the development of chronic disease. These biological changes are already apparent in young adults with a short history of alcohol consumption. A new study published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research found specific biomarkers of chronic disease across multiple biological systems related to both immediate and long-term alcohol use patterns.

mix_items.title: Targeting mosquitoes reduces flesh-eating ulcer risk in Melbourne trial
mix_items.summary: Mosquito control in an urban setting can reduce a person's risk of contracting Buruli ulcer by over 80%, finds a new Melbourne-led study.

mix_items.title: Could bats self-medicate? More than 50 wild bats offer clues
mix_items.summary: When humans get sick, we change our routines and try various solutions to feel better and get well, like staying in bed to rest, going to the doctor, getting medication from the pharmacy, using home remedies and more.

mix_items.title: Dark plasma regions reveal overlooked source of reactive atomic oxygen
mix_items.summary: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have found a way to make plasma more effective for its wide-ranging uses, from antimicrobial applications to surface conditioning in the semiconductor industry. They mapped the production of atomic oxygen, a key ingredient of oxygen plasma, while a high voltage was applied across oxygen gas.

mix_items.title: How the heart, lungs and brain work together to shape experience
mix_items.summary: People speak of "butterflies in the stomach," a "racing heart," being "choked up" or needing to "catch breath." Language routinely treats emotion and thought as though they inhabit the body. But why are events of the mind felt in the heart or stomach?

mix_items.title: Galileo, Copernicus, Cleansky, IRIS² must work together to secure Europe's place in the space race
mix_items.summary: "Seeing the Earth from above is a powerful reminder of our interdependence," said Thomas Pesquet. The words of France's 10th astronaut to head into space are a reminder of how we are "in this together," something the world's aerospace industry players should take heed of as they gather in Paris for the first International Space Summit from Sept. 9–10.

mix_items.title: Caregivers for people with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder report increased stress and relational strengths
mix_items.summary: Caregivers of people with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) identified stress levels and emotional health as the factors most negatively affected by their caregiving role. Many experienced limited social support and financial and employment challenges because of their caregiver role. These findings, just published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research, highlight the need for policies and programs that support families and caregivers of children and adults with developmental disabilities in general, and FASD in particular.

mix_items.title: Marine conservation collides with mining in Indonesia’s biodiversity-rich Moramo Bay
mix_items.summary: SOUTH KONAWE, Indonesia — A marine protected area in Indonesia’s Southeast Sulawesi province is home to a critically depleted population of humphead wrasse. The species presence helped the area gain its protected status, but mining permits overlap parts of the conservation zone and line its coast. mix_items.title: Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra
mix_items.summary: This gallery displays a collection of 16 galactic images from Chandra and other telescopes. Astronomers put galaxies into three main categories: spirals like our own Milky Way, ellipticals that are older and likely the results of mergers, and irregulars that can encompass a wide range of galactic phenomena. All types are represented in this collection. Each galactic image contains X-ray data from Chandra combined with data from telescopes such as NASA’s Webb, Hubble, IXPE, Swift, and NuSTAR, and others both in space and on the ground. The post Galaxy Gallery: Galactic Gems Glisten in New Gallery From NASA’s Chandra appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

satire_ro.title: Inspirat de programul „Școală după școală”, nea Costel lansează programul „Băut după băut”
